summary: Recommends retiring version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol and its dependent specifications, and explains why. It recommends moving RFC 1777, 1778, 1779, 1781 and 2559, and the documents they superseded, to Historic status.

eli5.summary: An old version of the directory lookup protocol was no longer a good idea. This note recommends officially putting it on the shelf as outdated.

questions: should i implement ldapv2 or ldapv3
subtitle: Why LDAP version 2 and the specifications built on it were recommended for retirement.

tldr.problem: LDAPv2 was not implemented the way its specification said, lacked adequate security, and had been superseded by LDAPv3.
tldr.mechanism: The document recommends moving RFC 1777, 1778, 1779, 1781 and 2559, and the older documents they superseded, to Historic status, and tells developers to implement LDAPv3 instead.
tldr.outcome: LDAPv2 and its dependent specifications are meant to be treated as retired. The document itself is Informational and not a standard.

today: RFC 3494 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It recommends that RFC 1777 and the related LDAPv2 documents be moved to Historic status, and points implementers to LDAPv3 (RFC 3377).

sections.title: What the Document Recommends
sections.content:
LDAPv2 (version 2 of the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) is an Internet protocol used to access X.500-based directory services. RFC 3494 recommends retiring it along with the specifications that depend on it: RFC 1777, RFC 1778, RFC 1779, RFC 1781 and RFC 2559, plus the documents they superseded.

LDAPv2 was published in 1995 as a Draft Standard. LDAPv3 was published as a Proposed Standard to resolve its inadequacies, and the text calls it clearly technically superior.
sections.eli5: An old way of asking a phone-book computer for information is being retired because a better way exists.

sections.title: Why LDAPv2 Is Not Followed
sections.content:
The RFC says LDAPv2 is not generally adhered to: an independently developed implementation of the specification would not interoperate with existing ones, which use different syntaxes and semantics. It gives two examples.

  • RFC 1777 and RFC 1778 require textual values to be IA5 (ASCII) or T.61 (Teletex), but implementations use ISO 8859-1, UCS-2, UTF-8 or the local character set.
  • RFC 1777 requires attribute type names from the X.500 standards, such as organizationName, but implementations use the LDAPv3 names, such as o.
sections.eli5: The rule book says one thing, but everyone actually plays by a slightly different set of rules, so a new player who follows the book would not be understood.

sections.title: Security and Dependent Specifications
sections.content:
LDAPv2 gives no mechanism for data integrity or confidentiality, and it does not support modern authentication such as DIGEST-MD5, Kerberos V or X.509 public keys. LDAPv3 offers far stronger options, and moving LDAPv2 to Historic may improve Internet security by encouraging use of LDAPv3.

Two dependent documents are affected. RFC 1781 (User Friendly Naming) relies on syntaxes from RFC 1779, and RFC 2253, which replaced RFC 1779, dropped them. RFC 2559, an applicability statement for using LDAPv2 with public key infrastructure, depends on RFC 1777, so it must move to Historic too.
sections.eli5: The old version has no lock on the door for sending secrets. The new version does, and pieces that only worked with the old one go to the shelf as well.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
Developers should not implement LDAPv2 per RFC 1777, because the result would not interoperate with existing LDAPv2 implementations. They should implement LDAPv3. Deployers should recognise the significant interoperability issues among current LDAPv2 implementations and use LDAPv3 instead.

The RFC recommends Historic status for RFC 1777, 1778, 1779, 1781 and 2559. The previously superseded RFC 1484, 1485, 1487 and 1488 (by RFC 1781, 1779, 1777 and 1778 respectively) should also become Historic.
sections.eli5: If you are building something new, use the new version. People already running the old one should switch.
